\smallskip

**Monthly background-check data, January 2000–December 2015**

## 1. Data and measurement

The CSV contains **`r shape[1]` rows, `r shape[2]` original variables, and `r missing` missing values**. Each row represents one geographic series in one calendar month. Each series has 192 consecutive months with no duplicates. The national series, `Totals`, already includes Missouri, Maryland, and New Jersey. Only the national rows enter Questions 2–8.

Estimated monthly sales are $Y_t=1.1(H_t+L_t)+2M_t^*$, where $H_t$ is `handgun`, $L_t$ is `longgun`, and $M_t^*$ is `multiple_corrected`. The correction excludes inconsistent California multiple-check data from the national calculation. The handgun and long-gun columns count category-specific FBI NICS checks. The corrected multiple-firearm column counts checks involving more than one firearm. The formula assigns 1.1 estimated firearms to each handgun or long-gun check and two to each corrected multiple check. Permit checks and other check categories are excluded. The weights approximate firearms per check, and some private transfers generate no check in the data (Aisch and Keller, 2016).

For January 2000, the national row gives $1.1(185{,}677+322{,}777)+2(7{,}826)=574{,}951.4$ estimated firearms. The decimal reflects the weighting rule. Adding the state rows to this total would count those states twice. I sorted by year and month before splitting the national series so each lag represents the correct number of months. The first 180 months determine every fitted coefficient and model choice. The final 12 months measure forecast accuracy.

## 2. The national series

```{r national}
style()
plot(d$date, d$y/1e6, type="l", col=teal, lwd=1.4, xlab="Year",
     ylab="Estimated sales (millions)")
abline(v=as.Date("2015-01-01"), lty=3, col=dark)
```

Mean monthly sales rose from `r fmt(mean(d$y[d$year==2000]))` in 2000 to `r fmt(mean(train$y[train$year==2014]))` in 2014. Late-year peaks recur, with particularly large observations in December 2012 (2.39 million), January 2013 (1.90 million), and December 2015 (2.35 million). The changing level and annual cycle violate the constant-mean assumption of an ordinary stationary ARMA model. The dotted line marks the start of the 2015 holdout.

The increase was uneven. Average monthly sales were about 588,000 in 2003, reached 1.28 million in 2013, and fell in 2014. Even within a single year, the series generally rises from summer into late fall. Fitting one constant mean to the raw data would therefore mix two different sources of apparent persistence. Adjacent months share a long-run level, and observations twelve months apart share a calendar position. I estimate those systematic differences first so that the ARMA coefficients describe what remains.

\newpage

## 3. The annual sales pattern

Mean monthly estimated sales in **thousands**, January 2000–December 2014 (15 observations per month):

```{r monthly, results='asis'}
means <- tapply(train$y, train$month, mean)
tab <- as.data.frame(t(round(means/1000)))
names(tab) <- month.abb
tableout(tab)
```

```{r seasonal-spread, fig.height=3.0}
style()
boxplot(I(y/1e6) ~ month, data=train, names=month.abb,
        xlab="Calendar month", ylab="Estimated sales (millions)",
        col="#D8EBED", border=dark, outline=TRUE)
points(12, train$y[train$date==as.Date("2012-12-01")]/1e6,
       pch=1, cex=1.65, lwd=1.8, col=rust)
```

The line in each box marks the median of that month's 15 training observations. The box spans the middle half of the values. The red ring marks December 2012. Comparing medians checks whether the seasonal contrast persists when an extreme observation has little influence. The December median is `r fmt(median(train$y[train$month.num==12]))` firearms, compared with `r fmt(median(train$y[train$month.num==6]))` in June. These summaries mix early and late years. Question 4 estimates the calendar effect while also accounting for the time trend.

December had the highest average and was the annual maximum in `r sum(tapply(train$y,train$year,which.max)==12)` of 15 years. November was next highest. June and July were nearly tied at the bottom. Recurrence across years identifies seasonality. December 2012 also exceeded the typical training December by `r fmt((d$y[d$date=="2012-12-01"]-means[12])/1e6,2)` million, illustrating how an exceptional month can coincide with a seasonal peak.

The table averages each January with other Januaries and likewise for each month, giving every training year equal weight. December averaged about 660,000 more estimated firearms than June. The 13 annual maxima matter because one large December can raise the December average, whereas it can change the identity of the highest month in only one year. For the exceptional observation, the relevant comparison is December 2012 against other Decembers. Comparing it only with summer would mix the unusual increase with the ordinary winter rise.

\newpage

## 4. Removing trend and seasonality

```{r decomposition, include=FALSE}
linear <- lm(y ~ t + month, data=train)
# Center in years to improve numerical conditioning of the quadratic.
train$u <- (train$t - mean(train$t))/12
test$u <- (test$t - mean(train$t))/12
trend <- lm(y ~ u + I(u^2) + month, data=train)
r <- as.numeric(resid(trend))
# Bartlett/Newey-West covariance with 12 monthly lags and n/(n-k) adjustment.
wald <- function(model, terms) {
  X <- model.matrix(model)
  scores <- X * as.numeric(resid(model))
  n <- nrow(X)
  S <- crossprod(scores)
  for (h in 1:12) {
    G <- crossprod(scores[(h+1):n,,drop=FALSE], scores[1:(n-h),,drop=FALSE])
    S <- S + (1-h/13) * (G+t(G))
  }
  B <- solve(crossprod(X))
  V <- n/(n-ncol(X)) * B %*% S %*% B
  j <- match(terms, colnames(X))
  b <- coef(model)[j]
  W <- drop(crossprod(b, solve(V[j,j,drop=FALSE], b)))
  c(W=W, p=pchisq(W,length(j),lower.tail=FALSE))
}
curve <- wald(trend,"I(u^2)")
train$cs <- cos(2*pi*train$month.num/12)
train$sn <- sin(2*pi*train$month.num/12)
season <- wald(update(trend, . ~ . + u:cs + u:sn), c("u:cs","u:sn"))
```

On the 180 training months, the required least-squares model is
$$\widehat Y_t=461{,}145+3{,}668.15t+\widehat\gamma_{m(t)},\quad \widehat\gamma_{\rm Jan}=0,$$
with $t=1$ in January 2000. Holding the month effect fixed, the fitted baseline increases by 3,668 estimated sales per month, or about 44,018 between successive Januaries. December's fitted adjustment is **+436,980 sales** relative to January at the same trend level. This is the calendar effect after controlling for time. For December and January of the same year, December is also 11 months later, so the fitted difference in this linear model is $436{,}980+11(3{,}668.15)\approx477{,}330$ estimated firearms.

```{r residual-comparison, fig.height=3.25}
style()
par(mfrow=c(2,1), mar=c(2.75,4.3,1.3,.8), mgp=c(1.85,.55,0))
for (item in list(list(linear,"Linear trend and month effects"),
                  list(trend,"Quadratic trend and month effects"))) {
  plot(train$date, resid(item[[1]])/1000, type="l", lwd=1.1, col=teal,
       ylim=c(-300,950), ylab="Residual (000s)", xlab="Year", main=item[[2]], cex.main=.95)
  abline(h=0,col="gray55",lty=2)
}
```

A residual is observed sales minus the fitted value for that month. A positive run means the baseline repeatedly underestimates sales. A well-chosen baseline can still leave an isolated spike, but a multi-year sequence of errors in the same direction suggests the assumed trend shape needs attention.

The linear fit leaves positive residuals early, mostly negative annual averages from 2003–2011, and a large positive cluster around 2013. To test for remaining curvature, let $u=(t-90.5)/12$ and add $u^2$. The null is a zero quadratic coefficient versus a nonzero coefficient. A Wald test gives $W=`r fmt(curve[1],2)`$ (1 df), $p=`r fmt(curve[2],5)`$. Both tests here use approximate chi-square reference distributions and a 12-lag Bartlett covariance estimate to allow serial correlation and unequal variance.

I retained the quadratic for Questions 5–8. Its January baseline is $706{,}962+44{,}018u+4{,}564u^2$, with separate month offsets. It reduces the broad curvature, although the late-2012 spike remains. Each calendar month's average training residual is zero by least squares, so retesting the same fixed month effects would be circular.

As a check on the size of the improvement, the root mean squared training residual falls from `r fmt(sqrt(mean(resid(linear)^2)))` to `r fmt(sqrt(mean(r^2)))` estimated firearms. Adding a term always weakly improves least-squares fit. The reason to keep this one is that a single curvature term addresses the multi-year pattern visible in the upper panel and the uncertainty-adjusted test supports it. Centering $t$ in years places $u=0$ near the middle of the training record, so the quadratic describes curvature around an observed period. Extrapolating assumes this same curvature continues into 2015.

Could the annual pattern itself change? I added $u\cos(2\pi m/12)$ and $u\sin(2\pi m/12)$ to the quadratic model. Under $H_0$ both coefficients vanish, versus at least one nonzero. The joint test gives $W=`r fmt(season[1],2)`$ (2 df), $p=`r fmt(season[2],4)`$. At 5%, there is evidence that the annual cycle changes over time. Fixed offsets remove average seasonality reasonably well, but miss some change in seasonal amplitude or timing.

The two interaction terms let a smooth annual wave change with time. This tests a feature that fixed month offsets cannot capture. I carry the quadratic plus fixed offsets forward as my forecasting baseline, and use the interactions as a diagnostic. The resulting forecasts assume a common calendar adjustment across years. The test gives a concrete reason that this assumption could hurt their accuracy.

## 5. Stationarity and remaining correlation

A weakly stationary process has finite second moments, a constant mean, and a covariance $\operatorname{Cov}(R_t,R_{t+h})=\gamma(h)$ depending only on lag $h$. In particular its variance $\gamma(0)$ is constant (course notes, Chapters 1–2). The lower panel in Question 4 varies around zero without the original upward drift. Runs of residuals with the same sign, larger late fluctuations, and the changing seasonal pattern qualify a stationary approximation.

```{r correlations, fig.height=2.15}
corplot <- function(x, partial=FALSE, title="", L=24) {
  values <- if (partial) as.numeric(pacf(x,lag.max=L,plot=FALSE)$acf) else
    as.numeric(acf(x,lag.max=L,plot=FALSE)$acf)[-1]
  plot(seq_len(L), values, type="h", lwd=1.7, col=teal, main=title, cex.main=.95,
       xlab="Lag (months)", ylab=if(partial) "Partial ACF" else "ACF",
       ylim=range(c(-.25,.25,values)), xaxs="i", xlim=c(0,L+1))
  abline(h=0,col=dark)
  abline(h=c(-1,1)*1.96/sqrt(length(x)),col=rust,lty=2)
}
style()
par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(3.3,3.8,1.5,.8))
corplot(r,title="Training residual ACF",L=36)
corplot(r,TRUE,"Training residual PACF",36)
```

The ACF starts at 0.80, 0.54, and 0.35, then decays and turns negative at intermediate lags. At 12 and 24 months it is 0.06 and $-0.07$ (PACF $-0.09$ and $-0.02$). Neither annual ACF stands out against the approximate white-noise guides ($\pm0.146$). Those guides are pointwise references, not formal tests for an already correlated series. The PACF is dominated by lags 1 and 2 (0.80 and $-0.27$). Persistence across nearby months is compatible with weak stationarity, which permits nonzero autocorrelations as long as they depend only on the lag. One finite realization cannot establish that population moments are constant across time.

**What the lags tell us.** A positive lag-1 ACF means that a month above its fitted baseline tends to be followed by another above-baseline month. The lag-2 ACF includes association transmitted through the intervening month. The lag-2 PACF asks what two months ago adds after accounting for last month. Its negative sign can therefore coexist with a positive lag-2 ACF. The small annual correlations give little reason to add a seasonal AR term solely because the original series had December peaks. They answer a different question from the changing-seasonality test in Question 4, which measured a systematic change in the mean seasonal pattern.

**Working decision.** I use an undifferenced residual model because deviations repeatedly return toward zero and the ACF declines quickly from its initial peak. Differencing these residuals would change the target to month-to-month changes in those deviations. There is less support for constant variance. The residual standard deviations for the first and last 90 training months are `r fmt(sd(head(r,90)))` and `r fmt(sd(tail(r,90)))` estimated firearms. That comparison is sensitive to the late spikes. I treat stationarity as a working approximation for point forecasts, with greater uncertainty about the size of exceptional errors.

\newpage

## 6. Three candidate models for the same residual series

```{r candidates, include=FALSE}
orders <- list("AR(2)"=c(2,0,0),"MA(2)"=c(0,0,2),"ARMA(1,1)"=c(1,0,1))
models <- lapply(orders,function(o) arima(r,order=o,method="ML",include.mean=FALSE))
stopifnot(all(vapply(models,function(x) x$code==0, logical(1))))
```

Each candidate explains the same 180 deviations from the quadratic and calendar-month baseline. I use the ACF and PACF patterns from Question 5 to choose a small order within each model family (Chapter 3, Lectures 11–14).

**Why these orders?** In a pure AR process the population PACF cuts off after its order. The sizable second partial correlation motivates allowing two previous residuals to enter directly. In a pure MA process the population ACF cuts off after its order because observations farther apart share no innovations. MA(2) tests whether the first two lags account for enough of the dependence despite the lag-3 ACF of 0.35. A mixed model can have tails in both plots. ARMA(1,1) is the smallest mixed model and allows the unusually strong first lag to differ from the later decay. Sample plots are noisy, so these patterns nominate candidates for fitting and checking.

Let $X_t=\widehat R_t$ in estimated firearms and $Z_t$ denote zero-mean white noise. Gaussian maximum likelihood fits use $d=0$ and a fixed zero mean because the regression centered the residuals. Under R's positive MA sign convention the fitted equations, with coefficients rounded to three decimals, are

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{AR}(2):\quad X_t &= 1.009X_{t-1}-0.266X_{t-2}+Z_t,\\
\mathrm{MA}(2):\quad X_t &= Z_t+0.982Z_{t-1}+0.402Z_{t-2},\\
\mathrm{ARMA}(1,1):\quad X_t &=0.682X_{t-1}+Z_t+0.343Z_{t-1}.
\end{aligned}$$

```{r fitted-table, results='asis'}
tableout(data.frame(Model=names(models),
  'Innovation variance (sales squared)'=fmt(sapply(models,function(m) m$sigma2)),
  AIC=fmt(sapply(models,AIC),2), check.names=FALSE))
```

**How to read the fitted equations.** In AR(2), increasing last month's deviation by 10,000 while holding the deviation two months ago fixed raises the next prediction by roughly 10,090. The negative second coefficient corrects for how much of that persistence was already evident two months earlier. In MA(2), a new positive innovation of 10,000 contributes about 9,820 one month later and 4,020 two months later. Its direct contribution ends there. In ARMA(1,1), the same innovation affects next month's forecast through both the observed deviation and the previous innovation, for an initial response of about $(0.682+0.343)10{,}000=10{,}250$. Further responses shrink by a factor of 0.682 per month.

Innovation variance measures the spread of the part left unpredictable one month ahead. Taking its square root puts the measure back in firearms. The fitted values are about 76,600 for AR(2), 81,400 for MA(2), and 76,400 for ARMA(1,1). AIC balances likelihood fit against the number of estimated parameters. All three candidates use the same response, months, mean convention, and parameter count, so their penalties are equal. MA(2)'s AIC exceeds the minimum by 22.30. AR(2)'s exceeds it by only 0.57. The next question checks whether the fitted innovations still contain a predictable pattern.

\newpage

## 7. Checking the candidate models

The diagnostic series now consists of each model's one-step prediction errors (innovations). A good fit should remove the short-lag dependence visible in Question 5. The panels show innovation autocorrelations on a common scale with approximate 95% pointwise white-noise guides.

```{r diagnostic-acfs, fig.height=2.1}
style()
par(mfrow=c(1,3),mar=c(3.3,3.5,1.5,.7),mgp=c(2,.52,0))
for (name in names(models)) {
  e <- as.numeric(resid(models[[name]]))
  a <- as.numeric(acf(e,lag.max=24,plot=FALSE)$acf)[-1]
  plot(1:24,a,type="h",col=teal,lwd=1.6,xlab="Lag (months)",ylab="ACF",
       ylim=c(-.45,.45),main=name,cex.main=.95)
  abline(h=0,col=dark)
  abline(h=c(-1,1)*1.96/sqrt(length(e)),lty=2,col=rust)
}
```

**Ljung–Box test at lag 24.** For each model, $H_0:\rho_1=\cdots=\rho_{24}=0$ for the innovations. Under $H_A$, at least one of these autocorrelations is nonzero. Each candidate estimates two AR/MA coefficients, giving $24-p-q=22$ reference degrees of freedom. A p-value is the approximate probability, under that model's null, of a $Q$ statistic at least as large as the observed one.

```{r ljung-box, results='asis'}
lb <- Map(function(model,o) Box.test(resid(model),lag=24,type="Ljung-Box",
                                     fitdf=sum(o[c(1,3)])), models,orders)
pval <- sapply(lb,function(x) x$p.value)
tableout(data.frame(Model=names(models),Q=fmt(sapply(lb,function(x) x$statistic),2),
                    df=sapply(lb,function(x) unname(x$parameter)),
                    'p-value'=formatC(pval,format="g",digits=4),
                    'Decision at 5%'=ifelse(pval<.05,"Reject","Fail to reject"),
                    check.names=FALSE))
eligible <- which(pval >= .05)
winner <- eligible[which.min(sapply(models[eligible],AIC))]
best <- models[[winner]]
```

**AR(2).** With $p=0.395$, the combined correlations are compatible with the null. Lag 19 barely crosses a pointwise guide. An isolated crossing among 24 lags can occur by chance.

**MA(2).** With $p=0.0000184$, a statistic this large would be very rare under the null. Several correlations, including lags 2 and 3, cross the guides. The short moving-average window leaves systematic dependence.

**ARMA(1,1).** With $p=0.329$, the test also fails to reject. Lag 19 crosses the lower guide, but there is little joint evidence of serial correlation through lag 24. Among the two models passing the diagnostic, ARMA(1,1) has the lowest training AIC (4565.94 versus 4566.51). I selected it before scoring 2015. The 0.57 AIC difference indicates little separation from AR(2).

**Why choose ARMA(1,1) when AR(2) has the larger test p-value?** The Ljung–Box test pools squared sample autocorrelations, with lag 24 covering two complete annual cycles. The p-value measures evidence against a model's zero-correlation hypothesis. Once both candidates pass this check, a larger p-value does not establish a better forecast. I use the lower AIC to break the tie. Both models have two dependence coefficients, their one-step error scales differ by only about 100–200 firearms, and neither shows a strong annual pattern in its innovation ACF. The choice is narrow enough that AR(2) remains a credible description of the training residuals. The selection uses no 2015 outcomes.

**Spikes remain.** The largest absolute innovation occurs in December 2012, about `r fmt(max(abs(resid(best)))/sqrt(best$sigma2),1)` fitted innovation standard deviations from zero. Weak residual autocorrelation can coexist with very large errors. The test addresses linear dependence, not normality, independence, or the cause of that spike.

In December 2012, observed sales exceeded the selected model's one-step prediction by about `r fmt(as.numeric(resid(best))[which(train$date==as.Date("2012-12-01"))])` estimated firearms. Accounting for December's usual level and recent positive deviations still leaves a large surprise. The one-step prediction uses earlier observations and parameters estimated over the full training period. It identifies an unusually large in-sample error. Only the 2015 forecasts below were scored on data excluded from estimation.

\newpage

## 8. Twelve forecasts from December 2014

```{r forecasting, include=FALSE}
residual.forecast <- as.numeric(predict(best,n.ahead=12)$pred)
forecast <- as.numeric(predict(trend,newdata=test)) + residual.forecast
last.year <- subset(train, year == 2014)
benchmark <- last.year$y[match(test$month.num, last.year$month.num)]
scores <- function(f) {
  error <- test$y-f
  c(MAE=mean(abs(error)), RMSE=sqrt(mean(error^2)))
}
```

Writing $T=180$ for December 2014, the two forecasting rules are
$$\widehat Y_{T+h\mid T}=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1 u_{T+h}
 +\widehat\beta_2 u_{T+h}^2+\widehat\gamma_{m(T+h)}+\widehat X_{T+h\mid T},
 \qquad \widehat Y^{\rm benchmark}_{T+h\mid T}=Y_{T+h-12}.$$
For horizon $h=1,\ldots,12$, the forecast is the fitted quadratic trend and month offset at $t=180+h$, plus the ARMA forecast of the residual at that horizon. Future innovations have conditional forecast zero. After the one-step forecast, the residual forecast decays by a factor of about 0.682 per month. The benchmark repeats the corresponding observed month of 2014. All forecasts use the same December 2014 origin.

```{r forecast-plot, fig.height=2.45}
style()
curves <- cbind(test$y,forecast,benchmark)/1e6
matplot(1:12,curves,type="o",pch=c(16,1,4),lty=c(1,2,3),lwd=1.6,
        col=c(dark,teal,rust),xaxt="n",xlab="2015",ylab="Estimated sales (millions)")
axis(1,1:12,month.abb)
legend("topleft",c("Observed","Trend + ARMA","Same month of 2014"),
       col=c(dark,teal,rust),lty=1:3,pch=c(16,1,4),bty="n",cex=.82)
```

For January, the deterministic component is `r fmt(as.numeric(predict(trend,newdata=test))[1])` and the predicted residual is `r fmt(residual.forecast[1])` estimated firearms. Adding them gives `r fmt(forecast[1])`. By December, the residual contribution is only `r fmt(residual.forecast[12])`, so the long-horizon model forecast depends almost entirely on the extrapolated baseline and the usual December offset. The seasonal benchmark instead starts from the observed level of each corresponding 2014 month. Neither method updates its forecast with actual 2015 sales as they arrive.

**Monthly results** (thousands of estimated firearms, rounded).

```{r monthly-forecasts, results='asis'}
half <- function(i) data.frame(Month=month.abb[i],Observed=round(test$y[i]/1000),
                                Model=round(forecast[i]/1000),Benchmark=round(benchmark[i]/1000))
monthly.results <- cbind(half(1:6), half(7:12))
knitr::kable(monthly.results, format="latex", booktabs=TRUE, row.names=FALSE,
             col.names=rep(c("Month","Observed","Model","Benchmark"),2))
```

**Errors over all 12 months** (estimated firearms, unrounded inputs).

```{r scoring, results='asis'}
score.table <- rbind('Trend + ARMA(1,1)'=scores(forecast),
                     'Same month of 2014'=scores(benchmark))
tableout(data.frame(Method=rownames(score.table), MAE=fmt(score.table[,1]),
                    RMSE=fmt(score.table[,2])))
```

For errors $e_h=Y_{180+h}-\widehat Y_{180+h}$, MAE averages $|e_h|$ and RMSE is the square root of the average $e_h^2$. **The same-month benchmark wins on both measures for 2015.** The model overpredicts January through November, then underpredicts December by about 508,000. Its December miss is smaller than the benchmark's roughly 651,000, but that advantage cannot offset the model's errors earlier in the year.

The benchmark cuts MAE by `r fmt(100*(1-score.table[2,1]/score.table[1,1]),1)`% and RMSE by `r fmt(100*(1-score.table[2,2]/score.table[1,2]),1)`%. MAE describes the average size of a monthly miss in firearms. RMSE gives large misses more influence because it squares each error before averaging. This explains why the benchmark's December miss narrows its advantage on RMSE. It still has smaller absolute errors in `r sum(abs(test$y-benchmark)<abs(test$y-forecast))` of the 12 months. The persistent overprediction fits the risk identified in Question 4. A quadratic estimated across the full training period projects continued growth, while the recent 2014 levels gave a closer reference for most of 2015. One holdout year cannot tell us whether that ranking will repeat.

## 9. Maryland around the 2013 policy event

Aisch and Keller (2016) identify May 2013 as the month Maryland approved new restrictions. The figure shows monthly state estimates from the project formula across 2012–2014. The dotted line marks May approval. The dashed line marks the October deadline discussed in the article. Plotting both dates lets us see whether the largest change coincided with approval or occurred in the intervening months.

```{r maryland, fig.height=1.95}
md <- subset(raw,state=="Maryland" & year>=2012 & year<=2014)
md <- md[order(md$date),]
style()
plot(md$date,md$y/1000,type="o",pch=16,cex=.5,col=teal,
     ylab="Estimated sales (000s)",xlab="Month",xaxt="n")
ticks <- seq(as.Date("2012-01-01"),as.Date("2014-07-01"),by="6 months")
axis.Date(1,at=ticks,format="%b %Y")
abline(v=as.Date("2013-05-01"),lty=3)
abline(v=as.Date("2013-10-01"),lty=2,col=rust)
legend("topleft", c("May approval","October deadline"),
       lty=c(3,2), col=c("black",rust), bty="n", cex=.78)
```

Estimated sales fell from 15,433 in May to 13,113 in July, then reached 52,798 in September before dropping to 21,381 in October. September was the final full month before the October deadline. The timing is consistent with buyers moving purchases forward, but these monthly counts contain no information about individual buyers’ motives. Maryland alone supplies no estimate of what September sales would have been without the policy. Nationwide demand, seasonal buying, or shifts in the timing of purchases could also affect the series.

I chose Maryland because the monthly approval date permits a before-and-after comparison within the event year. The surrounding years also let us compare September with the same calendar month. Maryland's September estimates were 10,220 in 2012, 52,798 in 2013, and 7,813 in 2014. The 2013 peak was more than five times the previous September's level. That comparison helps distinguish an exceptional September from an ordinary recurring fall peak. It still leaves open what would have happened in Maryland in 2013 under the same national conditions without the policy change.

## 10. Conclusions

The national series contains a recurring calendar pattern and a changing baseline. Across the training years, December averaged about 1.25 million estimated sales, more than twice the June average. Even against that high December baseline, the 2012 peak stands out. A linear trend left a long run of negative deviations in the middle years. Allowing curvature reduced that pattern, although the strength of the annual cycle also appears to change.

Departures from the fitted baseline persisted across nearby months. AR(2) and ARMA(1,1) both removed much of that dependence. The mixed model earned a narrow selection on training AIC. December 2012 still produced a one-step error about 7.3 innovation standard deviations above zero, even after accounting for recent months and the usual December peak. For 2015, extrapolating the fitted trend put forecasts above observed sales through November. Repeating the same month of 2014 reduced mean absolute error from about 235,000 to 108,000 estimated firearms. Both methods missed the December surge. A single test year establishes which method worked better in 2015 and leaves their longer-run ranking uncertain.

Two limitations affect interpretation. First, background checks measure transactions imperfectly. Some private sales are absent, and fixed conversion factors cannot recover how many firearms changed hands in each transaction (Aisch and Keller, 2016). Forecast errors therefore describe errors in the estimated series. Second, the Maryland comparison has no untreated comparison group. A spike following policy approval gives its timing, but concurrent national changes or buyers shifting purchases between months could produce a similar pattern.

# Measurements, annual levels, and seasonal contrasts

# Baseline coefficients, tests, and variation around the trend
print(coef(linear))
print(coef(trend))
print(list(curvature=curve, changing_season=season))
print(sapply(list(linear, trend), function(m) sqrt(mean(resid(m)^2))))
print(tapply(resid(linear), train$year, mean))

lags <- c(1,2,3,12,24)
print(data.frame(lag=lags, ACF=as.numeric(acf(r, plot=FALSE, lag.max=24)$acf)[lags+1],
                 PACF=as.numeric(pacf(r, plot=FALSE, lag.max=24)$acf)[lags]))

# Parameter estimates, remaining dependence, and the largest surprise
print(lapply(models, coef))
print(sapply(models, function(m) sqrt(m$sigma2)))
print(sapply(models, AIC) - min(sapply(models, AIC)))
print(names(models)[winner])
for (m in models) {
  a <- as.numeric(acf(resid(m), plot=FALSE, lag.max=24)$acf)[-1]
  print(which(abs(a) > 1.96/sqrt(length(resid(m)))))
}
e <- as.numeric(resid(best))
peak <- which.max(abs(e))
print(data.frame(date=train$date[peak], innovation=e[peak],
                 standardized=e[peak]/sqrt(best$sigma2)))

# Forecast components and performance on the original scale
print(data.frame(date=test$date, baseline=predict(trend,newdata=test),
                 residual=residual.forecast, forecast, benchmark, observed=test$y))
print(score.table)
print(100*(1-score.table[2,]/score.table[1,]))
print(sum(abs(test$y-benchmark) < abs(test$y-forecast)))
print(test$y - forecast)
